A horizon: The mineral soil layer near the surface, where organic matter mixes with sand, silt and clay. Its darker colour often reflects humus, but colour alone does not establish fertility or the depth of the layer.
Abrasion: The wearing away of rock by sediment carried against it by water, wind or ice. Look for scratches, polished surfaces or potholes. Unlike attrition, abrasion describes damage to the surface being struck, rather than collisions between transported particles.
Absorption: The transfer of radiation into a material, increasing its internal energy. Dark ground often absorbs more sunlight than bright snow. Absorption differs from reflection, which sends radiation away, and transmission, which lets it pass through.
Abstraction: The removal of water by people from a river, lake or aquifer for uses such as irrigation or drinking supplies. A store can shrink when abstraction and other losses exceed recharge, even though water continues circulating globally.
Active layer: The ground above permafrost that thaws in summer and freezes again in winter. Its thickness changes with local climate, vegetation and soil. Seasonal thaw of this layer does not necessarily mean that the underlying permafrost has disappeared.
Albedo: The fraction of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface, expressed from zero to one or as a percentage. Fresh snow usually has a high albedo and dark soil a lower one. Reflected energy in watts per square metre is a flux, not albedo itself.
Anticyclone: An atmospheric circulation around a region of high pressure, commonly associated with sinking air. Surface winds turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Clear skies are common, but fog and low cloud can persist.
Aquifer: A body of permeable rock or sediment that stores groundwater and allows useful amounts to flow through it. Water occupies connected pores or fractures; an aquifer is usually not an underground lake. Both storage space and connectivity matter.
Attrition: The breakdown and rounding of transported particles as they collide with one another. Pebbles may become smaller and smoother during repeated transport. This differs from abrasion, in which those particles wear away the bed, bank or another fixed surface.
B horizon: A subsurface soil layer modified by soil-forming processes, often with an accumulation of clay or iron compounds moved from above. Compare its colour and structure with the A horizon; a B horizon is not simply any material beneath topsoil.
Biological weathering: The breakdown or chemical alteration of rock caused by organisms. Roots can widen fractures, while organic acids from plants and microbes react with minerals. These effects overlap with mechanical and chemical weathering rather than forming an entirely separate mechanism.
Blockfield: An extensive cover of angular rock blocks, often found on cold upland plateaus. Frost action can contribute to its development, but the blocks may record a long history of weathering. Their presence alone does not prove that permafrost exists today.
Canary Current: The relatively cool eastern-boundary current flowing southward in the North Atlantic subtropical gyre. Coastal upwelling along northwest Africa can bring colder, nutrient-rich water to the surface. The current is a moving water mass, not simply a strip of cold weather.
Canyon: A deep valley with steep sides, commonly cut by a river into elevated rock. The surrounding plateau and the canyon are different landforms. Rock resistance, uplift and changing base level all influence how the valley develops.
Catena: A sequence of soils along a slope whose differences are related to relief, drainage and movement of sediment. Compare a freely drained crest with a wetter footslope. A catena need not form a perfectly regular sequence in every landscape.
Chemical weathering: The alteration or dissolution of minerals through chemical reactions with water, gases and dissolved substances. Carbonation, hydrolysis and oxidation are examples. Unlike mechanical weathering, these reactions change mineral composition as well as the appearance of the rock.
Clint: A block of limestone at the surface of a limestone pavement, separated from neighbouring blocks by enlarged joints called grykes. Rainwater containing weak carbonic acid dissolves the rock along those joints and can also carve grooves into each clint.
Colluvium: Loose sediment accumulated on or near the foot of a slope through gravity-driven movement and surface wash. It commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes. Unlike alluvium, it is not defined by deposition from a river channel.
Competence: The size of the largest particle that a flow can transport under given conditions. Faster, more forceful flow can generally move coarser material. Competence differs from capacity, which concerns the total amount of sediment a flow can carry.
Cone of depression: A lowering of the water table or groundwater pressure surface around a pumping well. Water flows towards the well down this hydraulic gradient. The cone is a pattern in water levels, not an empty cone excavated in the rock.
Confluence: The place where two streams or rivers meet. Downstream discharge usually includes water from both channels, although its timing depends on travel and storage. Sediment bars and mixing patterns may reveal the different flows at the junction.
Conformal: Describing a map projection that preserves local angles and small shapes. This is useful for bearings, but area can become strongly distorted over a world map. A conformal projection cannot also preserve the area of every region.
Constructive wave: A classroom description of waves that tend to build a beach because swash carries more sediment landward than backwash removes. Whether a beach actually grows also depends on sediment supply, slope and changing conditions over the whole wave cycle.
Continental drift: The movement of continents over geological time, proposed by Alfred Wegener using evidence such as matching fossils and rock belts. Plate tectonics later supplied a wider explanation: continents move as parts of lithospheric plates that also include ocean floor.
Contour: A line on a map joining points at the same height above a stated datum. Close contours usually indicate steep ground and wider spacing a gentler slope. A contour traces elevation, not a path that must be visible on the ground.
Contour interval: The vertical difference in elevation between neighbouring contour lines. Check the map key before calculating a slope or hill height. The interval stays fixed on many maps, while the horizontal spacing changes with the steepness of the terrain.
Convergence: The movement of air towards an area, bringing neighbouring flows together. Near the surface it can encourage rising air, cloud and rain if enough moisture is present. Convergence describes a flow pattern; it is not itself a type of cloud.
Convergent: Describing a plate boundary where plates move towards one another. Dense oceanic lithosphere may be subducted, while a continent–continent collision thickens the crust. The plate types determine whether a trench, volcanic arc or broad mountain belt develops.
Cover: Vegetation or plant residue that protects soil from direct raindrop impact and slows surface flow. Roots can also help hold particles together. The protective effect depends on the type, density and continuity of the cover.
Crown: The upper edge of a landslide, where displaced material separates from stable ground. Cracks near the crown can outline the developing failure. It is distinct from the toe, where displaced material accumulates farther down the slope.
Cut bank: The eroding outer bank of a river bend, where the faster part of the flow commonly approaches the bank. A steep face or exposed roots can reveal active erosion. Deposition often occurs on a point bar across the channel.
Day length: The time between sunrise and sunset at a place. It varies mainly with latitude and the time of year because Earth has a tilted axis. Day length differs from the approximately 24-hour solar day, which includes darkness.
Declination: The angular position of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator, equivalent to the latitude of the subsolar point. It varies between about 23.44° north and south through the year and helps determine noon altitude and daylight duration.
Deep water formation: The sinking of sufficiently dense surface seawater into deeper parts of the ocean. Cooling and increased salinity can contribute, especially at high latitudes. It is one part of a complex overturning circulation that also involves mixing and upwelling.
Deflation: The removal of loose surface particles by wind. Fine material may be carried away in suspension, leaving a coarser lag behind. Deflation removes sediment; abrasion is the wearing of surfaces by particles that the wind carries.
Divergence: The spreading of air away from an area. Surface divergence commonly accompanies sinking air in high-pressure systems, while divergence aloft can help sustain rising air below. Always state the height at which the flow is diverging.
Divergent: Describing a plate boundary where plates move apart. Mantle rock rises and can partly melt as pressure falls, producing new oceanic crust at ridges. Continental divergence may first form a rift before an ocean basin develops.
E horizon: A soil horizon depleted in materials such as clay, iron or organic compounds that have been carried away by percolating water. It often appears paler than adjacent layers. Not every soil profile contains a distinct E horizon.
Elbow of capture: A sharp bend marking where one drainage system has diverted water from another. It can help reconstruct river capture when combined with a wind gap or underfit valley. A sharp bend alone is not enough to prove capture.
Emission: The release of radiation by matter. Earth’s surface and atmosphere emit thermal infrared radiation at temperatures typical of this planet. This differs from reflection, which redirects incoming radiation without first absorbing it.
Energy budget: An accounting of energy entering and leaving a system, such as Earth or a patch of ground. A persistent imbalance changes stored energy and can cause warming or cooling. A surface budget also includes evaporation and sensible heat transfers.
ENSO: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a coupled pattern of ocean and atmospheric variability in the tropical Pacific. Its warm and cool phases alter sea-surface temperature, trade winds and rainfall. These phases influence weather probabilities rather than prescribing every local event.
Epicentre: The point on Earth’s surface directly above the focus of an earthquake. It helps locate an event on a map, but the strongest shaking may occur elsewhere because of fault rupture, distance and local ground conditions.
Equal-area: Describing a projection that preserves the relative areas of regions on a map. Shapes and angles must be distorted to achieve this on a flat surface. Equal-area maps are useful when comparing the size or distribution of geographic regions.
Equator: The circle at zero degrees latitude, halfway between the poles. It divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is a parallel of latitude, whereas meridians of longitude run from pole to pole.
Erg: A broad region covered by wind-deposited sand and dunes, often called a sand sea. An erg needs a supply of sand and conditions that allow it to accumulate. Many deserts instead have mainly rocky or gravel surfaces.
Evapotranspiration: The combined transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation and plant transpiration. It links soil moisture, vegetation and weather in a drainage-basin water balance. Potential evapotranspiration describes demand under adequate water supply, not necessarily the amount that actually occurs.
Eye: The relatively calm central region of a developed tropical cyclone, often with sinking air and reduced cloud. The surrounding eyewall contains much more vigorous convection and stronger winds. Passing into the eye does not mean that the storm has ended.
Eyewall: The ring of deep convection around a tropical cyclone’s eye, usually containing its strongest winds and heaviest rainfall. Its position and structure can change as the storm evolves. It differs from the calmer eye and the outer spiral rainbands.
Falling limb: The part of a hydrograph after its peak, when discharge decreases as stored water drains from a catchment. Its shape reflects delayed flow from soil, groundwater and channels. Rain may have stopped well before river discharge returns to its earlier level.
Fissure eruption: An eruption in which magma emerges along an elongated crack rather than only from a single central vent. Lava fountains may form a line and then become concentrated at a few outlets. Basaltic fissure eruptions are common in Iceland and Hawaiʻi.
Focus: The point within Earth where an earthquake rupture starts, also called the hypocentre. Rupture can then spread across a much larger fault surface. The epicentre is the point directly above it at the surface.
Föhn / chinook: A warm, often dry wind descending on the sheltered side of a mountain range. Air warms as it is compressed during descent, and moisture loss or differences in source air can intensify the effect. Föhn and chinook are regional names.
Foliation: A planar fabric in metamorphic rock, formed by aligned minerals or compositional bands. It commonly develops under directed stress. Foliation differs from sedimentary bedding, although both may appear as layers in an outcrop.
Footwall: The block of rock below an inclined fault plane. Identify it from the geometry of the plane before describing movement. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall; reverse motion is the opposite.
Four-figure grid reference: A reference identifying a 1 km square on a standard British National Grid map by its southwest corner. Read the easting first and then the northing. It identifies a square, not an exact point within it.
Friction: Drag between moving air and the surface, which slows the wind and changes its direction. Near the ground this allows wind to cross isobars towards lower pressure. Higher in the atmosphere, surface friction is much weaker.
Geostrophic wind: An idealised wind in which the pressure-gradient force is balanced by Coriolis acceleration, so flow runs parallel to straight isobars. It is most useful above the frictional surface layer and away from the equator.
Glacial rebound: The gradual rise of land following the removal of a large ice load. The solid Earth adjusts as mantle material flows slowly over time. Rebound changes relative sea level locally, even while global mean sea level may rise.
Gorge: A narrow, steep-sided valley. One way it can develop is through the retreat of a waterfall, leaving a deeply cut channel downstream. The surrounding rock and the river’s erosive history control its form.
Groyne: A structure extending across a beach to interrupt longshore sediment movement. Sand may build up on its up-drift side while the down-drift beach receives less. Its effects should be considered within the wider coastal sediment budget.
Gryke: A deepened joint or fissure separating clints on a limestone pavement. Weakly acidic water dissolves limestone along the fracture and widens it. Plants often occupy grykes because they trap soil and offer shelter.
Gyre: A large-scale rotating system of ocean currents. Winds, Earth’s rotation and the shapes of ocean basins help organise subtropical gyres. A gyre includes currents with different widths, speeds and temperatures rather than one uniform loop.
Hadley cell: The average tropical circulation in which air rises near the equatorial convergence zone, moves poleward aloft and descends in the subtropics. Near-surface return flow contributes to the trade winds. The real circulation shifts with seasons and continents.
Hanging valley: A tributary valley whose floor lies above the floor of the main glacial trough. The larger glacier commonly erodes more deeply than its tributary. After ice retreat, a waterfall may connect the two valley levels.
Hanging wall: The block above an inclined fault plane. In a normal fault it moves downward relative to the footwall, while in a reverse fault it moves upward. The names describe position relative to the plane, not present elevation.
Headward erosion: The extension of a valley or channel back towards its source by erosion. Over time it can shift a drainage divide and help one river capture another’s headwaters. It describes growth upstream, not water flowing uphill.
Helicoidal flow: A secondary, spiral-like circulation within a river bend, superimposed on the downstream current. Near-bed movement helps transfer sediment towards the inner bank, while strong flow near the outer bank promotes erosion. The pattern varies with channel shape and discharge.
Hydraulic action: Erosion caused by the force of moving water, including pressure fluctuations and water or trapped air acting within cracks. It can loosen material from a riverbank or coast. Abrasion adds the separate effect of sediment striking those surfaces.
Igneous: Describing rock formed when magma or lava cools and crystallises. Slow cooling underground commonly produces larger crystals than rapid cooling at the surface. Texture therefore offers evidence of cooling history, although composition also affects the minerals present.
Inner core: Earth’s solid central region, composed mainly of an iron-rich alloy and extending about 1,220 km from the centre. High pressure keeps it solid despite its temperature. It is surrounded by the liquid outer core.
Insolation: Incoming solar radiation received at a surface. Its amount depends on the angle of the Sun, daylight duration and atmospheric conditions. Insolation is an energy input; air temperature also depends on energy losses, storage and transport.
Interception: The temporary capture of precipitation on leaves, branches and other surfaces before it reaches the ground. Some water evaporates and some drips or flows down stems. Interception changes the timing and amount of water entering soil.
Interfluve: Higher ground between neighbouring river valleys or channels. Its slopes shed water towards the adjacent channels. An interfluve may lie within a larger drainage basin and is not necessarily the boundary of that entire basin.
Inverse barometer: The tendency for sea level to rise where atmospheric pressure falls, and fall where pressure rises. A rough equilibrium estimate is about 1 cm per hectopascal. Storm surge also depends strongly on winds and coastal geometry.
Isostasy: The gravitational balance in which the lithosphere is supported by denser material beneath it. Adding or removing a large load causes deformation and adjustment over time. The mantle flows slowly as solid rock rather than as a simple liquid ocean.
Köppen: A climate classification system that groups places by long-term monthly temperature and precipitation. Its letter codes describe climatic thresholds and seasonality. Vegetation can suggest a climate, but one landscape or one day’s weather cannot determine the classification.
Lapse rate: The rate at which temperature changes with height in the atmosphere. An environmental lapse rate describes measured surrounding air; an adiabatic rate describes a rising or sinking parcel. An inversion occurs where temperature increases with height.
Limestone pavement: An exposed limestone surface divided into blocks called clints and solution-enlarged joints called grykes. Glacial stripping can expose the rock, after which chemical weathering enlarges fractures. The pavement records both exposure and later dissolution.
Lithification: The conversion of loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock, commonly through compaction and cementation. Pressure reduces pore space, while minerals can precipitate between grains. Lithification does not normally require the sediment to melt.
Lithosphere: Earth’s rigid outer mechanical layer, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle. It is divided into tectonic plates and overlies the weaker asthenosphere. The lithosphere is therefore thicker than the crust alone.
Long profile: A plot of a river’s elevation against distance downstream. Many profiles become gentler towards the mouth, but resistant rock and uplift can interrupt a smooth curve. It differs from a cross-profile drawn across a valley.
Longshore drift: The net movement of beach sediment along a coast as oblique waves drive swash up the beach and gravity returns backwash downslope. Direction depends on wave approach. Structures that interrupt the supply can change beaches farther along the coast.
Longwave: Thermal infrared radiation emitted by Earth’s surface and atmosphere. It generally has longer wavelengths than most incoming solar radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and emit parts of this spectrum, influencing the rate at which energy escapes to space.
Magnitude: A measure of an earthquake’s overall size, commonly reported as moment magnitude based on fault area, slip and rock rigidity. One event has a magnitude, while its shaking intensity varies from place to place. The scale is logarithmic.
Mantle: The rocky layer between Earth’s crust and core, extending to about 2,900 km depth. It is predominantly solid but can deform and circulate very slowly. Small amounts of partial melt occur in particular settings; it is not a global magma layer.
Mechanical weathering: The physical breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without changing its mineral composition. Frost action and expansion or unloading can contribute. The fragments remain near their source until erosion transports them away.
Mercator: A conformal cylindrical map projection on which constant compass bearings plot as straight lines. It is useful for some navigation tasks, but areas become greatly enlarged towards the poles. Apparent land areas on it should not be compared directly.
Metamorphic: Describing rock changed by heat, pressure or chemically active fluids while remaining mostly solid. New minerals or fabrics may develop. If the material melts and then crystallises, the resulting rock is igneous instead.
Neap tide: A period of relatively small tidal range, usually near the first and third quarters of the Moon. The Sun’s and Moon’s tide-generating effects partly oppose one another. Local coastal geometry and tidal timing modify the range observed.
Nick point: An abrupt steepening in a river’s long profile, also written knickpoint. A waterfall is one example. Resistant rock, uplift or a change in base level can produce one, and erosion may cause it to migrate upstream.
Nival: Describing a river regime strongly influenced by seasonal snowmelt. Discharge often increases during the thawing season. This differs from a glacial regime dominated by the melting of glacier ice.
Normal fault: A fault on which the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall. It commonly forms where the crust is being extended. Determine movement from displaced layers rather than the present height of the land surface alone.
O horizon: A soil layer dominated by organic material such as leaf litter and decomposing plant remains. It may overlie mineral horizons in some soils but be absent in others. Its thickness depends on inputs, decomposition and disturbance.
Onshore flow: Air moving from the sea towards land. It can occur in a local sea breeze or within a larger weather system. The term describes direction relative to the coast, not a fixed compass bearing.
Orogeny: A period or process of mountain building involving deformation and thickening of the crust. Plate collision and subduction are common settings. Mountains may later be eroded, leaving folded rocks and other evidence of an older mountain belt.
Orographic rainfall: Precipitation associated with air being lifted over high ground. Rising air expands and cools; if it becomes saturated, cloud can form and precipitation may follow. The lee side may receive less rain, depending on the wider weather pattern.
Oxisol: A deeply weathered soil order common in humid tropical regions, typically rich in iron and aluminium oxides. Long weathering and leaching can leave a low supply of readily available nutrients. A red colour alone is insufficient for classification.
Partial melt: Melting of only part of a rock, because its constituent minerals do not all melt under the same conditions. Melt may separate and rise while solid material remains. This helps explain why magma differs in composition from its source rock.
Phase: The fraction and shape of the Moon’s sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth as viewing geometry changes through its orbit. Ordinary lunar phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow; that shadow is involved in a lunar eclipse.
Pirate stream: The stream that gains water by capturing the headwaters of another drainage system. It may extend its valley by headward erosion. The term describes a changed drainage connection, not a different type of flowing water.
Plain: A broad area of relatively low relief, often but not always at low elevation. Plains can form by deposition, erosion or other processes. Flatness alone does not identify how a particular plain developed.
Plateau: An extensive area of elevated, relatively level ground. Rivers can dissect it into deep valleys and canyons while remnants of the high surface remain. A plateau describes broad relief rather than a particular rock type.
Polar cell: The average circulation in which cold air sinks near a pole and moves equatorward near the surface, returning poleward aloft. It forms part of a simplified global circulation model. Actual polar weather is less uniform than a single closed loop.
Pothole: A rounded hollow eroded into a rocky riverbed by turbulent water and circulating sediment. Trapped stones may assist abrasion as water swirls. It differs from a large plunge pool formed directly beneath a waterfall.
Pressure gradient: The change in atmospheric pressure over a given distance. A larger gradient exerts a stronger pressure-gradient force on air. Closely spaced isobars often indicate a strong gradient, but wind also depends on friction and Earth’s rotation.
Pyroclastic: Describing fragmented volcanic material ejected during an explosive eruption, including ash, lapilli and larger blocks. Pyroclastic deposits differ from coherent lava flows. Particle size and deposit structure help reconstruct how material was transported.
Quadrature: The arrangement in which the Sun and Moon appear about 90 degrees apart from Earth, near a quarter Moon. This geometry is associated with neap tides, although local tides respond with delays and are shaped by their ocean basin.
R horizon: Hard bedrock beneath a soil profile. It differs from loose or partly weathered parent material usually labelled the C horizon. Roots and water may still penetrate joints even where the rock remains consolidated.
Radiosonde: An instrument package carried by a balloon that measures atmospheric properties such as temperature, humidity and pressure as it rises. Tracking its position also reveals winds. A sounding is a vertical sample at a time and place, not a complete atmospheric map.
Rain shadow: A relatively dry area on the sheltered side of high ground. Uplift and precipitation can remove moisture from approaching air, while descending air warms and its relative humidity falls. Prevailing winds influence the strength of the effect.
Rain splash: The detachment and movement of soil particles by raindrop impact. It can begin erosion before continuous runoff develops. Vegetation, litter and surface roughness reduce the direct impact on exposed mineral soil.
Recharge: The addition of water to an aquifer, usually as infiltrated rainfall or surface water percolates downwards. Recharge may take time and vary strongly by season and geology. It is not identical to all rainfall falling on the land above.
Resurgence: A place where water that flowed underground returns to the surface, often as a spring in karst terrain. Tracer studies can link a resurgence to a distant sinking stream. The visible outlet does not reveal the whole underground route.
Reverse fault: A fault on which the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall, commonly under compression. A low-angle reverse fault is called a thrust. Displaced rock layers help identify motion even after erosion changes the surface.
Rill: A small channel cut into soil by concentrated surface runoff. Rills can often be removed by ordinary cultivation, unlike larger gullies. They show that water has begun collecting into preferred routes rather than flowing as a broad sheet.
Rising limb: The part of a hydrograph during which river discharge increases towards a peak. Its steepness reflects how quickly water reaches the channel. A rapid rise can follow intense rain or efficient runoff from saturated or paved surfaces.
Root: In isostasy, the thickened lower part of continental crust beneath a mountain belt. Less dense crust extends deeper into the mantle and helps support high topography. The term describes crustal structure, not a literal plant-like shape.
Rotation: The spinning of a body around its own axis. Earth’s rotation produces the day–night cycle and contributes to the apparent daily motion of the sky. It differs from revolution, which describes orbital motion around another body.
Salinity: The concentration of dissolved salts in water. Evaporation and sea-ice formation can raise seawater salinity, while rainfall, river inflow and melting ice can lower it. Salinity and temperature together strongly influence seawater density.
Sea breeze: A local wind blowing from sea towards land when daytime heating makes the land warmer than nearby water. A circulation develops with rising air over land and return flow aloft. Stronger background winds can weaken or overwhelm it.
Sediment budget: An accounting of sediment entering, leaving and being stored within a defined area. A beach can erode when losses exceed supply, even if deposition occurs briefly. State the boundaries and time period before comparing inputs and outputs.
Sedimentary: Describing rock formed from accumulated sediment or from chemical or biological precipitation. Clastic sediments commonly become rock through compaction and cementation. Bedding, grains and fossils can preserve evidence of the depositional environment.
Shortwave: Radiation at the shorter wavelengths that carry most incoming solar energy, including visible light and parts of the ultraviolet and infrared spectrum. Earth’s much cooler surface emits mainly longwave radiation instead. Shortwave does not mean visible light alone.
Six-figure grid reference: A reference locating a 100 m square within a standard British National Grid kilometre square. Read three easting figures before three northing figures. Adding figures improves reference precision, but the map and observation still limit accuracy.
Slip-off slope: The gently sloping inner bank of a river bend, where sediment tends to accumulate as a point bar. It contrasts with the steeper outer cut bank. Both develop as the bend migrates and its flow redistributes sediment.
Snowmelt: Water released when accumulated snow changes from solid ice to liquid. Seasonal snowmelt can produce a strong spring or summer rise in river discharge. Its timing depends on temperature, radiation, elevation and snowpack depth.
Solar altitude: The angle of the Sun above the observer’s horizon. A higher Sun concentrates a beam over a smaller horizontal area and shortens a vertical object’s shadow. Altitude depends on latitude, date and time of day.
Solar day: The time between successive passages of the Sun across the local meridian, averaging 24 hours. It is slightly longer than a sidereal day because Earth also moves along its orbit while rotating.
Solstice: The time when the Sun reaches its greatest northerly or southerly declination. It corresponds to the longest or shortest daylight period of the year outside the tropics. Opposite hemispheres experience opposite seasonal solstices.
Spot height: The stated elevation of a particular point on a map, usually measured above a specified vertical datum. It provides a labelled value where contours show broader relief. It does not give the height of every nearby point.
Spring line: A line of springs where groundwater emerges along a geological or topographic boundary, often where permeable rock meets less permeable material. Its position reflects underground flow paths and can help explain the location of settlements.
Spur: A ridge projecting from higher ground between valleys. Contours commonly form V or U shapes pointing downhill along it. In a stream valley, equivalent contour bends usually point uphill, helping distinguish the two on a map.
Stage: The height of a river’s water surface above a specified gauge datum. Stage can be converted to discharge using a calibrated rating relationship, but they are different measurements. Changes in the channel can alter that relationship.
Stalactite: A mineral deposit hanging from a cave roof, commonly formed when dripping water loses carbon dioxide and precipitates calcite. A stalagmite grows upward from the floor. Neither feature is formed by limestone simply melting.
Store: A quantity of material or energy held within part of a system, such as water in a lake or carbon in vegetation. Inputs and outputs change the amount stored. A store is an amount; a flux is a transfer rate.
Storm surge: A rise in sea level above the expected tide, driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Coastal shape and water depth influence its size. Surge combines with tides and waves to determine coastal water levels and flooding.
Stratosphere: The atmospheric layer above the troposphere, extending roughly to 50 km altitude. Temperature generally increases with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. This stable layering limits the vertical mixing typical of the lower weather layer.
Stump: The low remnant of an eroded sea stack, often visible only at low tide. Wave action and weathering reduce the isolated rock over time. The cave–arch–stack–stump sequence is useful, although real coasts can follow more complicated histories.
Surface trace: In the fronts lab, the line where a sloping boundary between air masses meets Earth’s surface. It is plotted using weather observations. The edge of a visible cloud band may lie elsewhere and does not locate the front precisely.
Synodic month: The time from one lunar phase to the next occurrence of the same phase, averaging about 29.5 days. It is longer than the Moon’s orbital period relative to the stars because Earth also moves around the Sun.
Ternary plot: A triangular diagram showing three proportions whose sum is 100%. Each corner represents one pure component. In the soil-texture triangle, a sample’s sand, silt and clay percentages locate its texture class.
Terrestrial planet: A planet with a predominantly rocky composition and a solid surface, such as Mercury, Venus, Earth or Mars. The category describes composition rather than habitability. These planets differ greatly in atmosphere, temperature and geological activity.
Texture: In soil science, the proportions of sand, silt and clay in the mineral fraction. Texture influences pore sizes, drainage and water retention. It differs from soil structure, which describes how particles are arranged into aggregates.
Thermal circulation: A circulation driven by differences in heating and the resulting pressure and density patterns. A sea breeze is a local example, with rising air over warmer land. Rotation and background winds alter larger-scale circulation.
Till: Unsorted sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, often containing a mixture from clay to boulders. Its poor sorting distinguishes it from many meltwater deposits reworked by flowing water. Till can form several types of glacial landform.
Toe: The downslope end of a landslide or other mass-movement deposit. Displaced material may thicken or bulge there as it slows. It differs from the crown, where material separates from the stable slope.
Transfer: The movement of material or energy between stores within a system. In a drainage basin, infiltration transfers water from the surface into soil. A transfer describes a pathway or process; a flux quantifies its rate.
Transform: Describing a plate boundary where neighbouring plates slide horizontally past one another. Crust is neither systematically created nor consumed along the boundary. Earthquakes are common because friction allows stress to build before fault slip.
Tributary: A stream or river that joins a larger channel at a confluence. Its flow and sediment contribute to the downstream river. A tributary can have its own drainage basin nested within the larger river system.
Tropical cyclone: An organised, rotating low-pressure system with a warm core that develops over tropical or subtropical water. Strong storms can form an eye and eyewall. Hurricanes and typhoons are regional names for the same class of storm.
Tsunami: A series of long waves generated by rapid displacement of water, most commonly during a large undersea earthquake. In shallow water they slow and can grow in height. Tsunamis are not caused by the normal daily tides.
U-trough: A valley with a broad floor and steep sides produced or enlarged by glacial erosion. It contrasts with the narrower V-shaped cross-section often associated with river incision. Later rivers and slope processes continue modifying the glacial valley.
V-valley: A valley with a broadly V-shaped cross-section, commonly developed where river downcutting and slope processes work together. Its form depends on rock, climate and erosion history. A V shape is evidence to interpret, not proof of one process acting alone.
Vine–Matthews: The hypothesis linking symmetrical seafloor magnetic anomalies to spreading at ocean ridges and reversals of Earth’s magnetic field. Newly cooled crust records the field at formation. Comparing anomaly sequences with reversal ages provides evidence for plate movement.
Walker cell: A simplified east–west tropical Pacific circulation, with rising air over warmer water and sinking air over cooler water. Its near-surface branch is linked to the trade winds. Changes in this circulation are part of ENSO.
Warm front: The boundary where a warmer air mass advances over colder air near the surface. Gradual uplift can produce extensive layered cloud and precipitation. The exact weather depends on moisture, stability and the larger storm system.
Wind gap: A valley crossing a drainage divide that no longer contains the stream that cut it. It can be evidence of river capture or another drainage change. Compare its shape with neighbouring valleys and the present stream network.
Wind setup: A rise in water level where persistent wind pushes water towards a shore. It contributes to storm surge, particularly over shallow shelves and within bays. Its size depends on wind, duration, depth and coastal shape.
Windward: The side of a feature that faces the approaching wind. Moist air forced upward there may form cloud and rain. Windward is relative to wind direction, so it does not always mean the same compass-facing slope.
Yardang: An elongated ridge shaped by wind erosion in relatively soft material, typically aligned with the prevailing erosive wind. Abrasion and deflation carve the surrounding grooves. A yardang is an erosional landform, unlike a dune built by deposition.
Continentality: The influence of distance from the ocean on a place’s climate. Inland locations often have larger seasonal temperature ranges because land heats and cools faster than water. Prevailing winds, elevation and nearby currents also affect the contrast.
Eastern boundary current: A current along the eastern side of an ocean basin, such as the Canary Current. In subtropical gyres these currents are usually broader, slower and cooler than western boundary currents, and coastal winds can also support upwelling.
Ecliptic: The plane of Earth’s orbit around the Sun, projected onto the sky as the Sun’s apparent annual path. The Moon’s orbital plane is inclined by about five degrees to it, so most new and full Moons do not produce eclipses.
Evaporative cooling: Cooling that occurs when evaporation uses energy from a surface and its surroundings. A moist surface can lose energy as latent heat instead of warming. The effect depends on available water, humidity, wind and incoming energy.
Gas giant: A large planet made mainly of hydrogen and helium, such as Jupiter or Saturn. These planets have deep atmospheres above increasingly dense interiors and lack a solid surface like Earth’s. Their visible bands and storms occur within the atmosphere.
Gully: A channel cut into soil or unconsolidated material by concentrated runoff, larger and more persistent than a rill. In agricultural settings, a gully is generally too large to be removed by ordinary tillage and can expand through further erosion.
Hill: An area of raised ground with relief above its surroundings, generally smaller than a mountain. Shape and local context matter: there is no universal height that separates the two. Contours can show its summit, slopes and relative height.
Horizon: A layer within a soil profile distinguished by properties such as colour, texture, organic matter or mineral accumulation. Horizons develop through soil-forming processes. Their boundaries can be gradual, and a real profile need not contain every named horizon.
International Date Line: The conventional boundary across which the civil calendar date changes, located broadly near 180 degrees longitude. Its course bends around countries and islands for practical reasons. It differs from the prime meridian, which defines zero longitude.
Intraplate volcanism: Volcanic activity occurring within a tectonic plate rather than along its boundary. Hawaiʻi is one example. Possible causes include mantle upwelling and lithospheric processes; its location alone does not establish the depth or structure of the magma source.
Isobar: A line joining places with the same atmospheric pressure on a weather chart. Closely spaced isobars indicate a large pressure gradient over a given distance. Wind also responds to Earth’s rotation and friction, so it does not simply follow that gradient.
Knoll: A small, usually rounded hill standing above nearby ground. On a contour map it commonly appears as nested closed lines with increasing elevation towards the centre. Read the height labels to distinguish it from an enclosed depression.
Latitude: The angular position of a place north or south of the equator, expressed in degrees. Latitude helps determine solar altitude and seasonal day length. Lines of equal latitude are parallels, unlike meridians, which measure longitude.
Longitude: The angular position of a place east or west of the prime meridian, expressed up to 180 degrees. Earth turns through approximately 15 degrees per hour, linking longitude with local solar time. Civil time zones also reflect administrative choices.
Magnetic reversal: A change in the polarity of Earth’s magnetic field. Magnetic minerals in cooling volcanic rock can preserve the field’s direction at the time they formed. Reversals occur at irregular intervals, so magnetic bands do not all represent equal durations.
Magnetic stripe: A band of oceanic crust whose magnetic minerals record a particular field polarity. Seafloor spreading carries newly formed crust away from a ridge, producing broadly matching polarity sequences on its two sides. Stripe widths also depend on spreading rate.
Mass movement: The downslope movement of rock or soil under gravity, including falls, slides and flows. Water can increase weight or pore pressure and may be mixed with the moving material. Gravity provides the driving force rather than a transporting river or wind.
Meridian: A line of longitude running from one pole to the other. A place’s local solar noon occurs when the Sun crosses its local meridian. Meridians meet at the poles, so the distance between adjacent longitudes decreases towards high latitudes.
Mouth: The place where a river enters a sea, lake or another river. Its form depends on sediment supply, water movement and local topography. Some mouths build deltas, while others form tidal estuaries or enter a larger channel directly.
Nabkha: A mound of windblown sediment accumulated around a shrub or other vegetation. The plant slows nearby airflow and traps moving grains. Its shape and growth reflect the interaction between vegetation, wind and sediment supply rather than wind direction alone.
Node: One of the two places where the Moon’s orbital plane crosses Earth’s orbital plane. Eclipses require a new or full Moon close enough to a node for the Sun, Earth and Moon to align within the relevant shadow.
Noon altitude: The Sun’s angle above the horizon at local solar noon. In a simple geometric calculation it is 90° minus the absolute difference between latitude and solar declination. A negative value means the Sun remains below the horizon at noon.
Northing: A map-grid coordinate measuring distance north from the grid’s defined origin. Read it after the easting when giving a grid reference. The coordinate locates a position within a projected grid; it is not the same quantity as latitude.
Occlusion: The process in which a cold front catches up with a warm front and lifts the intervening warm air away from the surface. The resulting occluded front can have extensive cloud and precipitation, depending on the air masses involved.
Oceanic crust: The outer rocky layer beneath most ocean basins, composed mainly of basalt and gabbro and averaging about seven kilometres thick. It forms at spreading ridges and is eventually recycled at subduction zones. It is only part of an oceanic plate.
Orbital inclination: The angle between an orbital plane and a chosen reference plane. The Moon’s orbit is inclined by about five degrees to Earth’s orbital plane. This usually carries the Moon above or below the alignment required for an eclipse.
Orbital period: The time taken for a body to complete one orbit around another body. Planets farther from the Sun generally have longer periods: Mercury takes about 88 days and Neptune about 165 years. This differs from the body’s rotation period.
Ozone layer: A region of the stratosphere with a relatively high concentration of ozone. Absorption of ultraviolet radiation helps warm this layer and reduces the amount reaching the ground. It is a diffuse region of gas, rather than a solid protective shell.
Pangaea: A supercontinent assembled during the late Palaeozoic and broken apart during the Mesozoic. Its reconstruction uses evidence from rocks, fossils, magnetism and continental margins. Pangaea was one of several supercontinents in Earth’s history, rather than Earth’s original crust.
Parallel: A line joining places at the same latitude. On a spherical globe, the equator is the largest parallel and the others become smaller towards the poles. Parallels do not intersect, unlike meridians of longitude, which meet at the poles.
Passive margin: A transition between continental and oceanic crust that is not an active plate boundary. Many Atlantic margins developed after continental rifting. Sediment accumulation, subsidence and occasional earthquakes can still occur, so passive does not mean completely inactive.
Periglacial: Describing processes and landforms associated with cold ground, including freeze–thaw, frost sorting and thermal cracking. They may occur near glaciers or far from present ice. Relict features can remain after a region’s climate has become warmer.
Perihelion: The point in an orbit where a body is closest to the Sun. Earth reaches perihelion in early January. The changing distance affects incoming solar energy, while Earth’s axial tilt explains the opposite seasons of the two hemispheres.
Plunge pool: A deep hollow at the foot of a waterfall, enlarged by turbulent water and sediment striking the bed. Undercutting and collapse may contribute to waterfall retreat. The pool’s form also depends on rock structure, discharge and sediment supply.
Projection: A mathematical method for representing positions on a curved surface on a flat map. Every world projection changes some combination of area, shape, distance or direction. Its suitability depends on which properties matter for the map’s intended use.
Rainband: An elongated or curved band of showers and thunderstorms within a storm system. Tropical cyclones commonly have spiral rainbands outside the eyewall. Their rainfall and winds can affect locations well beyond the eye, with large variation between storms.
Revolution: The movement of one body around another along an orbit. Earth completes a revolution around the Sun in approximately one year. Rotation is the separate movement around its own axis, which produces the daily cycle of daylight and darkness.
Rotational slump: A landslide in which a mass of soil or rock rotates along a curved slip surface. The upper part commonly drops and tilts back, while material moves outward near the toe. Water pressure can reduce the slope’s resistance to failure.
Seafloor spreading: The formation and outward movement of oceanic crust at a spreading ridge. Magma cools to form new crust as the plates separate. Increasing rock ages and broadly matching magnetic polarity sequences on either side provide evidence for this process.
Shear surface: A surface along which adjacent masses move relative to each other. In a landslide it separates moving material from the underlying slope and may be curved or nearly planar. It is distinct from the exposed cliff or landslide scar.
Shelf: The shallow, gently sloping submerged edge of a continent, extending towards a steeper continental slope. Shelf depth and shape influence tides, waves and storm surge. A shallow shelf can support greater wind-driven water-level rise for the same forcing.
Sidereal day: The time Earth takes to complete one rotation relative to distant stars, approximately 23 hours and 56 minutes. The mean solar day is longer because Earth also moves along its orbit and must turn farther to face the Sun again.
Source: The starting point of a river’s channel, which may be a spring, a lake outlet or the convergence of small flows. The river also receives water along its course, so its source is not its only water input.
Spreading rate: The speed at which plates separate at a spreading ridge, usually expressed in centimetres per year. A full spreading rate measures separation across both sides; a half rate measures one side’s motion relative to the ridge, so the convention matters.
Spring tide: A tide with a relatively large range, occurring around new and full Moon when solar and lunar tide-generating effects reinforce each other. Spring refers to the larger tidal range, rather than the season. Local coastlines and basins modify the response.
Subtropical high: A region of relatively high atmospheric pressure commonly found near the poleward side of the Hadley circulation. Descending air tends to suppress cloud formation, helping explain many subtropical dry regions. Its position and strength vary with season and geography.
Sun path: The apparent arc followed by the Sun across the sky during a day. Its height, direction and duration above the horizon depend on latitude and date. Comparing paths explains seasonal changes in daylight and in the length of shadows.
Supercontinent: A large assembly containing most of Earth’s continental landmasses. Geological evidence records several episodes of assembly and breakup, including Pangaea. Their histories involve different oceans, plate boundaries and timescales rather than a perfectly repeating arrangement.
Surface wave: A seismic wave that travels along Earth’s surface, including Love and Rayleigh waves. These waves can produce strong, prolonged ground motion, although damage also depends on frequency, distance, ground conditions and buildings. They differ from body waves travelling through Earth.
Syzygy: An approximately straight-line alignment of three celestial bodies. In the Sun–Earth–Moon system it occurs around new and full Moon and contributes to spring tides. An eclipse also requires sufficiently close alignment with the relevant orbital node and shadow.
Tidal range: The vertical difference between a high tide and the neighbouring low tide at a location. It generally increases around spring tides and decreases around neap tides. Coastal shape, water depth and basin resonance strongly influence the local range.
Trade winds: The prevailing tropical surface winds blowing towards the equatorial convergence zone. Earth’s rotation gives them an easterly component: they generally come from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere. Their position and strength vary seasonally.
Tropics: The region between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, approximately 23.44 degrees north and south. The Sun can be directly overhead only within this belt, on dates determined by latitude. Tropical climates still vary greatly in rainfall and elevation.
Umbra: The central part of a shadow where the light source is completely obscured. During a total lunar eclipse the Moon lies within Earth’s umbra. The surrounding penumbra receives light from part of the source and produces a less complete darkening.
USDA texture triangle: A chart used to classify soil from its percentages of sand, silt and clay. The three fractions must add to 100%, and their intersection identifies a texture class. Texture describes particle size, while structure describes how particles form aggregates.
Valley: An elongated area of low ground between higher slopes, often containing a stream or river. Water and ice can create different valley cross-sections. Where contours cross a stream valley, their bends generally point upstream towards higher ground.
Viscosity: A measure of a fluid’s resistance to deformation and flow. Magma viscosity depends on composition, temperature and crystal content. More viscous magma can hinder gas escape, but eruption style also depends on gas supply, ascent and interaction with external water.
Water table: The upper surface of an unconfined groundwater body, below which connected pores are saturated. Its height changes with recharge and groundwater flow. In a confined aquifer, the level reached in a well represents pressure head rather than a free water table.
Wavelength: The distance between corresponding points on successive waves, such as one crest and the next. A tsunami has a very long wavelength compared with ordinary wind waves. Its wavelength changes as speed and water depth change during propagation.
Weathering (to sediment): The breakdown or alteration of rock in place, supplying particles and dissolved material that may enter sedimentary pathways. Erosion then removes material, transport carries it, and deposition stores it elsewhere. These are connected processes rather than interchangeable names.
Westerlies: The prevailing winds with a west-to-east component across much of the middle latitudes. They help steer many weather systems, although individual winds change as pressure systems move. Their average pattern reflects atmospheric circulation and Earth’s rotation.
Western boundary current: A narrow, fast current along the western side of an ocean basin’s subtropical gyre, such as the Gulf Stream or Kuroshio. These currents generally carry warm water poleward. Western refers to the ocean basin, not the coast of the neighbouring continent.
Wilson cycle: A framework describing the opening and eventual closing of an ocean basin through rifting, seafloor spreading, subduction and continental collision. Different basins follow different histories. Geological structures can preserve evidence of stages even after an ocean has disappeared.
